title: Message queues
objective: Use a queue to absorb bursts and decouple producers from workers, and handle messages that keep failing.

sources.title: AWS documentation: Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017): message brokers and stream processing

simplifies: Each message takes 100 ms of work (illustrative); a poison message always fails; retries go to the back of the queue straight away. Real queues add visibility timeouts, delays between retries (backoff), ordering rules and delivering a message more than once, which is why workers should be idempotent.

challenges.title: Absorb a burst
challenges.prompt: A burst triples traffic for 4 seconds, 3 seconds in. Keep rejections at 1% or less the whole time for 8 seconds.

predict.prompt: The queue holds only 20 messages. When the burst hits, what happens?

options.text: It fills up and new messages are rejected
options.explanation: Right. Messages arrive faster than workers clear them, and a small queue overflows.
Workers have fixed speed; the queue is what absorbs the difference.
A burst three times the normal rate has to go somewhere.

challenges.hint: The workers can catch up after the burst, if the messages have somewhere to wait.
challenges.explain: A bigger queue holds the burst and lets the workers catch up afterwards. Nothing is rejected, but messages wait longer: watch the slowest 5% go up. A queue trades waiting for refusing.

challenges.title: Keep up
challenges.prompt: 30 messages a second arrive steadily. Keep the slowest 5% of waits at 1 second or less for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: Two workers can clear about 20 messages a second. With 30 arriving, what happens to the queue?

options.text: It grows and grows, and waits keep getting longer
options.explanation: Right. A queue only buffers; if arrivals beat the workers for good, the backlog never shrinks.
Ten more arrive every second than leave.
It can't empty while more arrive than leave.

challenges.hint: A queue can't fix too little capacity. What does?
challenges.explain: More workers raise how fast messages leave. With four, the queue stays short and waits stay low.

challenges.title: Poison messages
challenges.prompt: 8% of messages always fail, and failures are retried. Keep the slowest 5% of waits at 1 second or less for 10 seconds.
challenges.hint: Retrying forever means the same broken messages keep coming back. Where could they go after a few tries?
challenges.explain: After 3 failed tries, a dead-letter queue sets the message aside for a person to look at, so workers stop spending their time on it and the queue drains.

quiz.prompt: What does a queue between producers and workers give you?

options.text: Producers don't wait for workers, and bursts are smoothed out
options.explanation: Right. It decouples the two sides, as long as on average the workers keep up.
Each message takes just as long; the queue changes when it is processed.
Queues can still reject when full, and failures need handling.

quiz.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue for?

options.text: Messages that keep failing, so they stop blocking the rest
options.explanation: Right. They wait aside for inspection instead of being retried forever.
It frees workers from hopeless retries, but doesn't make them faster.
